title: Classical Algorithms for Function Computation in Gaussian Boson Sampling
authors: Ruoting Dou, Hao Zhan, Shengjun Wu, Lijian Zhang, Penghui Yao
abstract: Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) seeks quantum advantage by sampling photon-number patterns generated with squeezed inputs and passive linear optics. Many proposed GBS applications instead target function computation by applying functions to mode-resolved photon-number outcomes---a natural form of experimental postprocessing that produces classical outputs. Sampling hardness alone, however, does not determine the complexity of these tasks. By analyzing the irreducible decomposition of fixed-photon-number operator spaces, we prove that the expectation value of every such function in the average case over passive linear-optical networks can be classically evaluated for inputs with finite squeezing strength. We also provide a classical algorithm that estimates this value to inverse-polynomial additive error. The result provides new theoretical tools for analyzing linear-optical quantum systems, helps clarify the origin of current GBS hardness evidence, and inspires new applications of GBS with genuine quantum advantages.
summary: This paper analyzes function computation in Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) by focusing on the average expectation value of functions applied to photon-number outcomes. The authors prove that for finite squeezing, this average value can be efficiently estimated classically. This work refines the understanding of GBS complexity by distinguishing between sampling hardness and the complexity of calculating specific function averages.
main_problem: The paper addresses whether function computation based on mode-resolved photon-number outcomes from Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) can be classically evaluated, moving beyond merely establishing sampling hardness.
main_result: It proves that the average-case expectation value of such functions can be classically estimated with high accuracy for inputs with finite squeezing strength.
method: The analysis uses operator space decomposition into irreducible U(m)-submodules and develops randomized classical polynomial-time algorithms based on Monte Carlo estimation.
model_or_system: The system is Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) implemented with squeezed-vacuum states injected into a passive linear-optical network, followed by photon-number-resolving detection.
key_observables: The expectation value $\mu_f(U) := \mathbb{E}_{s \sim P_U} [f(s)]$ of a function $f$ applied to mode-resolved photon-number outcomes.
important_parameters: Finite squeezing strength ($r_{	ext{max}} < \infty$), system size ($m$), and the required estimation error ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the function $f$ is polynomial-time evaluable on recorded PNR outcomes and that the squeezing strength is finite.
figures_summary: TABLE I compares the resource boundary for different GBS variants, highlighting the novel area of 'Function-average estimation' achieving 'Efficient classical estimation'.
paper_structure: The structure involves decomposing the operator space into correlation orders ($V_{n,k}$), deriving error bounds based on this decomposition, and finally constructing a classical Monte Carlo algorithm to estimate the expectation value by truncating the infinite sum.
why_interesting: It provides new theoretical tools for analyzing linear-optical quantum systems, clarifying the conditions under which GBS hardness might fail for specific types of post-processing measurements.
